newsitem.title: CONGO: FEATURE - Afrikaners eye maize belt from Congo to the Cape.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Afrikaners eye maize belt from Congo to the Cape.

text.p: In the days of French Equatorial Africa, the Congo's Niari Valley produced all the manioc served from Libreville to N'Djamena.
Now there's an idea that those 80,000 hectares of laterite could supply maize as far south as Cape Town.
A group of Afrikaner farmers settled in the Niari 18 months ago at the invitation of the Congo.

The Congolese needed help in farming more intensively and overhauling existing food processing plants, and Pretoria knew it would probably have to start importing food before 2015 to satisfy domestic demand.
Rapid population growth, coupled with a lack of fertile farmland and a series of droughts since 1992 are behind the anticipated South African food supply problem.

"At the 25-year horizon it wouldn't surprise me if they're going to require imports, grains in particular," said Tim Dyson who specializes in sub-Saharan African food production at the London School of Economics.

South Africa was still producing more grain than it was consuming in 1990. However, the United Nations projects the country's population in 2020 will be vastly higher than in 1990 and nothing in recent harvests indicates production could rise at the same rate.

"For the moment we're self-sufficient, but we take the long-term strategic view that in 15 to 20 years time part of our food needs will come from Zambia, Zimbabwe and Central Africa," said Jan van Deventer, South Africa's ambassador to Congo and Zaire.
FOOD FOR CENTRAL AFRICA
Yet the immediate aim of the farmers in the Niari is to produce food for Central Africa.

"The aim is to feed the Congo and neighbouring countries," said Johann van der Westhuizen, the Executive Chairman of the South African Devlopment Corp., the Pretoria-based private company that is the Congolese government's partner in the Niari project. He said he is keen to expand the operation, but he first wants to see it working on its current scale.
The Niari isn't the only region of Central Africa attractive to South African farmers, but the situation is delicate.

"There's sensitivity in Pretoria as the government doesn't want to be seen as exporting jobless South Africans, in particular whites," van Deventer said, adding that was why private-sector initiative was preferred.
The South Africans stressed their aim is not only to grow crops but also to set up development projects with the locals.
Conversely, the private enterprise nature of the project limits the help the South African government can give the farmers with settling in.
There is sensitivity on the Congolese side too. The Congo only established diplomatic relations with South Africa in March 1993 after the abolition of apartheid.
Recent political tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali over the rebellion in eastern Zaire haven't made things any easier.
STILL SETTLING IN
It will be some time before the 20 or so families who have settled in the Niari start producing food for export.
Most are still bringing in equipment and building homes. Some underestimated the difficulties of adapting to their new conditions.
"There will be growing pains -- there are growing pains but no serious ones," van Westhuizen said.
Settling in would probably have been easier had the Congo been a former British colony rather than a French one, diplomats said, citing communication and cultural problems.

Other countries where South African farmers have settled include Zambia and Mozambique. Zaire was keen to attract settlers, but political instability there has meant South Africa has shown little interest. A project in Gabon has been examined.
The South Africans also have more experience of conditions that prevail in Zambia and Zimbabwe than in Central Africa.
"There's interest in all these countries, but some are more suitable than others," said van Deventer.
